quote: “We know her woof, her texture,” says Keats—an interesting use of the word “we,” because I suspect that Keats didn’t know the explanation himself.
content: The lines are spoken by the narrator of Lamia at the moment the philosopher Apollonius exposes the serpent-woman, and the poem’s plot is on philosophy’s side: Lamia is an illusion, the young man Lycius is being deceived, and the “cold philosophy” that unweaves her is telling the truth. Critics since Bate’s biography (1963) have read the passage as deliberately double-voiced, a complaint the poem stages and then undercuts, rather than Keats’s manifesto. The suspicion about Keats’s ignorance is addressed in the annotation on Fake Reductionism: he was a licensed apothecary with a hospital training in chemistry. And the essay’s own thesis, joy in the merely real, has no better exemplar in English than Keats’s “To Autumn,” a poem that consists entirely of a catalogue of common things (gourds, hazel shells, gnats, lambs, a cider press) and finds them sufficient. The poet chosen as the anti-reductionist foil wrote the definitive poem of the essay’s position, and the essay does not seem to know it.

quote: Or go about the rest of your life suffering from existential ennui that is unresolvable.
content: The dichotomy assumes that one’s metaphysics is what determines one’s capacity for joy, and the data on well-being say it mostly is not. Across the large cross-national surveys, the association between religiosity and well-being is present in countries where life is difficult and religion is normative and absent or reversed in secure, secular societies (Diener, Tay & Myers (2011)); the secular Nordic populations are among the highest in life satisfaction on every measure, with no evident epidemic of unresolvable ennui; and what predicts well-being at the individual level is social connection, health, income security and temperament, not whether one has decided that rainbows are allowed to be real. The essay may be right that an attitude of appreciation toward explained things is available and worth cultivating. It is not right that the alternative is a life of existential ennui, and the picture of the naturalist as someone who must actively choose joy or be “disappointed in everything” is the Romantic picture with the sign flipped: it grants Keats the premise that disenchantment is the default, and then argues one’s way out. Most non-believers report no such default to escape.

quote: You might say that scientists—at least some scientists—are those folk who are in principle capable of enjoying life in the real universe.
content: This is a claim about the affective lives of scientists compared to others, and it is not tested here or, to my knowledge, anywhere. What has been measured points to the opposite of exceptionalism: scientists’ rates of depression and anxiety are high in the doctoral population (Evans et al. (2018) found graduate students six times as likely as the general population to report moderate-to-severe anxiety and depression), and the interest in pocket lint or rainbows the essay describes is the ordinary human trait of curiosity, present in children of every background before schooling selects who becomes a scientist. The essay’s picture, in which the capacity for joy in the real is a rare disposition that scientists happen to have and world-weary sophisticates lack, is a flattering self-description of the essay’s intended audience, and the flattery is the only evidence offered for it.
